description: Multi-dimensional adversarial review of a diff or capability: correctness, security, and spec compliance, with every finding adversarially verified before it is reported.

args.scope: fix-restore-schema-drift backend (tools/restore.mjs: Flyway version check, backend restart after restore, storage note)
args.focus: Operator tooling in tools/ (plain Node), run on Windows and POSIX; the IT runs a separate compose project. Check the restart/health-wait logic, failure exits after the restore committed, and that nothing touches the owner doucko stack.

findings.title: Unguarded JSON.parse in the health wait can crash with a stack trace after the restore has committed
findings.evidence: `backendHealthy()` runs `.flatMap((line) => JSON.parse(line))` on `docker compose ps --format json` stdout and nothing catches it. If one line is not JSON (a partial line, a plugin notice on stdout, or a compose release with another format), Node exits with an uncaught SyntaxError. The operator then sees a stack trace instead of the designed message saying the data is restored, followed by the manual `docker compose restart backend` step. Design decision 3 says every failure after the commit should print that message.
findings.suggestion: Wrap the parse in try/catch. On a parse error, either `continue` (retry until the deadline) or return false so the existing `fail(...)` path prints the data-is-restored message and the manual step.

findings.title: Reading the checkout's migrations is not guarded and can throw after the commit
findings.evidence: `const latest = latestMigration();` calls `readdirSync(MIGRATIONS_DIR)` only after `restore complete` has been printed. If that directory is missing or unreadable (a sparse or partial checkout, or a moved tools/ copy), ENOENT is thrown uncaught. The exit code is non-zero, but the output is a stack trace, not the message that the data is restored and the backend may need a restart.
findings.suggestion: Read `latestMigration()` before the destructive step so a broken checkout fails with "nothing was changed". Or catch the error and call `fail()` with the manual-restart hint.

findings.title: Message for a schema that is still behind after the restart can name the wrong cause
findings.evidence: `const migrated = schemaVersion(); if (!migrated || compareVersions(migrated, latest) < 0) fail(`...schema is at ${label(migrated)}...: its image is older than this checkout. Rebuild...`)`. `schemaVersion()` returns `undefined` when psql fails (for example, a db hiccup right after the restart). The message would then say "schema is at an unreadable version ... its image is older than this checkout" and send the operator to rebuild the image for what is really a read failure.
findings.suggestion: Handle `migrated === undefined` separately: say the version could not be read and print the manual check or restart hint. Keep the "image older than this checkout" text for a version that was read and is still behind.

findings.title: Logs hint on restart failure leaves out the compose project
findings.evidence: The failure text says "Check `docker compose logs backend`, fix the cause and run `${manualRestart}`". `manualRestart` includes `-p <project>` when `--project` is set, but the logs command does not. With a non-default project, running that logs command as printed (and without `-f` to the repo's compose file) targets the default `doucko` project. That is the owner's stack, not the one that failed.
findings.suggestion: Build the logs hint the same way as `manualRestart`, e.g. `docker compose${opts.project ? ` -p ${opts.project}` : ""} logs backend`, and share that prefix between both hints.

findings.title: Health wait retries silently when `docker compose ps` keeps failing
findings.evidence: `if (r.status !== 0) continue;` retries every 2 s for up to 300 s without any output. If compose cannot list the service (daemon gone, wrong project), the operator waits 5 minutes with no feedback. The final message then says the backend "did not come back healthy", which hides the real cause: compose could not be queried.
findings.suggestion: Count consecutive `ps` failures and fail early with a specific message ("docker compose could not report the backend's state") plus the manual-restart hint. Or print a short progress line while waiting.

findings.title: Migration IT builds a full backend image inside the IT run, so the test is heavy and slow
findings.evidence: `run("docker", "compose", "-p", project, "build", "backend", timeoutSec = 1200)` builds the backend image from the Dockerfile on every run, and `--rmi local` removes it in tearDown. Isolation from the owner's image holds: the image is named `<project>-backend` and only that project's local images are removed. The cost is up to 20 minutes per `verify`, and a docker build failure (e.g. a network problem fetching Maven dependencies) fails NFR-10 for reasons that have nothing to do with restore.
findings.suggestion: Consider building the image once per test class, or tagging it per run and reusing it, or putting this scenario behind an opt-in profile. Keep the separate project and `--rmi local` cleanup as they are.

findings.title: A dump with tables but no flyway_schema_history counts as 'behind' and restarts a working backend into a crash loop
findings.evidence: `behind` is true when `restored === null` (no flyway_schema_history), so if the backend is running, restore.mjs:158 restarts it. application.yaml has no `baseline-on-migrate`, so Flyway refuses a non-empty schema that has no history table. The backend then fails at startup and `restart: unless-stopped` keeps restarting it. The operator ends up with a restarted backend in a crash loop where before there was a running one. The tool does exit 1 (via backendHealthy → 'restarting'/'unhealthy'), but the restart already happened. Trigger: restoring a hand-made or foreign pg_dump that has tables but no Flyway history.
findings.suggestion: Restart only when there is a Flyway history (`restored !== null`), or when the public schema is empty. If the database has tables but no history, warn and don't restart: Flyway can't adopt that schema without a baseline.

findings.title: The target version comes from the checkout, not the running image, so a checkout older than the image leaves a mismatched schema and exits 0
findings.evidence: `latestMigration()` reads src/main/resources/db/migration in the working tree. Example: the image was built at V5, then the operator checked out an older branch whose migrations end at V4, and the dump is at V4. `behind` is false, so nothing restarts, and the tool prints success with exit 0. The running V5 backend then serves a V4 schema, and requests that touch V5 tables return 500s. That is exactly the failure this change is meant to prevent. The post-restart check at line 166 covers the opposite case (image older than checkout) but not this one.
findings.suggestion: Read the expected version from the running backend instead of the checkout, for example with `docker compose exec backend` to list the migrations in the jar, or from an actuator/flyway or info endpoint. At minimum, when the backend is running, restart it whenever the restored version differs from the version that was there before the restore.

findings.title: An uncaught JSON.parse in the health wait prints a stack trace after the restore has committed and loses the 'data is restored' message
findings.evidence: backendHealthy() calls `JSON.parse(line)` on each stdout line of `docker compose ps --format json` with no try/catch. If a compose release or plugin writes non-JSON to stdout, Node throws, prints a stack trace and exits 1 after the single-transaction restore has already committed. The operator never sees the `fail()` text saying the data is restored and that they should run `docker compose restart backend`. That is the guidance this change adds, and the 'usage, not a stack trace' style is what OperatorToolGuardTest enforces for this tool elsewhere.
findings.suggestion: Wrap the parse in try/catch and treat unparseable output like a failed `ps` (continue polling). Or run the whole post-commit section inside one try/catch that calls `fail()` with the manual-restart message.

findings.title: Checklist coverage for this diff: the security areas are clean (informational)
findings.evidence:
Each checklist item, checked against this diff:
(1) Authz/IDOR/tenant scoping: no HTTP endpoints changed. The IT only reads GET /api/child/hq inside its own project. Clean.
(2) Auth/sessions: untouched. The IT passwords are throwaway test values ('it-only-*'). Clean.
(3) Injection: every docker/psql call uses spawnSync argv with no shell. `--project` goes in as a single argv element (compose.mjs composeArgs). The SQL strings are constants. The dump reaches the container as an fd on stdin. `manualRestart` is only printed, never executed. Clean.
(4) Exposure: compose.yaml is unchanged. The backend and db are still unpublished. Clean.
(5) Privacy/legal: the IT uses the fictional name 'Hrdinka' and overrides the owner's .env DOUCKO_CHILD_DISPLAY_NAME. No workbook content was added. Clean.
(6) Secrets: no secrets in the diff or in the tool output. The psql queries print only Flyway versions. Clean.
(7) Dependencies: no package.json or pom.xml changes, and tools/lib/migrations.mjs has no dependencies. npm audit was not run, because no dependencies changed.
(8) Abuse resistance/rate limits: not applicable (local operator CLI).
Owner-stack isolation holds: the IT always passes `-p doucko-it-<uuid>`. Because compose.yaml sets `build: .` with no `image:` and no explicit volume `name:`, the image and volumes are project-scoped. `down -v --rmi local` therefore removes only `<project>-backend` and the IT volumes, never `doucko-backend`, doucko-pgdata or doucko-storage.
Restart/health-wait logic: `continue` still runs the sleep in the update expression, the 300 s deadline outlasts the container healthcheck's 150 s to unhealthy, a 'restarting' state is treated as failure, and every exit after the commit goes through `fail()` with the manual step (except the JSON.parse case above).
findings.suggestion: Nothing to change beyond the three findings above.

findings.title: Coverage summary: 6 scenarios: 5 implemented, 1 partial, 0 missing, 0 contradicted (plus one clause in the requirement text that the code contradicts, see below)
findings.evidence: Scenarios 1-4 (backup survives volume loss, broken dump changes nothing, older dump over newer schema, unsafe backup targets) are covered by the existing BackupRestoreIT/OperatorToolGuardTest. 'A dump from before the newest migration under a running backend' is implemented (tools/restore.mjs:686-703) and tested (BackupRestoreIT.kt:442-461). 'Restored schema and checkout disagree without a restart' is implemented (restore.mjs:674-685), but the test only partly asserts it. NFR-10 traces to the plan's platform-foundation/backend row. There is no OpenAPI impact: tools/ only, no src/main change.
findings.suggestion: Informational. Act on the individual findings below.

findings.title: Task 3.5 'Archive; commit' is ticked, but the change is not archived
findings.evidence: tasks.md: '- [x] 3.5 Archive; commit with `Slice: fix-restore-schema-drift` + `Refs: NFR-10`.' Reality: the change still sits at openspec/changes/fix-restore-schema-drift/ with no archive/2026-10-05-fix-restore-schema-drift folder. The diff's own traceability-report.md:110 adds 'active change "fix-restore-schema-drift" is not archived', and trace.json has the same warning. Only the commit trailer part is done (HEAD has Slice/Refs).
findings.suggestion: Run `openspec archive fix-restore-schema-drift` so the MODIFIED 'Data volume and backup' requirement lands in the spec, or untick 3.5 until that is done.

findings.title: Task 3.3 is ticked, but review-findings.json does not exist
findings.evidence: tasks.md: '- [x] 3.3 Review (fresh reviewer); every finding dispositioned in `review-findings.json`.' The change folder holds only proposal.md, design.md, tasks.md and specs/. There is no review-findings.json, while every archived change (e.g. archive/2026-10-05-implement-practice-flow-api/review-findings.json) has one.

findings.title: Task 3.1 'qa:verify green' points at verification evidence this change did not regenerate
findings.evidence: tasks.md 3.1: '[x] `npm run qa:verify` green. Evidence: `docs/qa/automated-verification-latest.md`.' The file is not in `git diff 394ed08..HEAD --stat`, and it says 'Started: 2026-10-05T07:19:49Z' (09:19 Prague). The replay evidence in the same change has dump timestamp 20261005-172607, so the battery output does not clearly cover the final tools/restore.mjs. Per the done-claims-need-evidence lesson, the pointer must be fresh.
findings.suggestion: Re-run `npm run qa:verify` on HEAD and commit the regenerated docs/qa/automated-verification-latest.md, or untick 3.1.

findings.title: The 'schema still behind after restart' failure path omits the manual restart step and the 'data is restored' message
findings.evidence: Spec: '...it SHALL restart the backend, wait until it is healthy and confirm the schema reached the newest version, or else print the manual restart step and exit non-zero'. Design decision 3: 'Every failure after the restore committed (... schema still behind) prints that the data IS restored plus the manual `docker compose [-p <project>] restart backend` step'. Code: fail(`the backend restarted, but the schema is at ${label(migrated)}, not V${latest}: its image is older than this checkout. Rebuild and start it with npm run stack:up.`). It contains neither manualRestart nor 'the data is restored'. Also, when --project is set, `npm run stack:up` would act on the default (owner) stack, not that project.
findings.suggestion: Prefix the message with 'the data is restored, but'. Either amend the spec/design to say this branch prints the rebuild step instead of the restart step, or include a project-aware rebuild command such as `docker compose -p <project> up -d --build backend`.

findings.title: The post-commit failure branches (exit 1 + manual step) have no test
findings.evidence: Spec clause: 'or else print the manual restart step and exit non-zero'. The evidence file admits: 'The failure branches after the restore committed (restart fails, healthcheck turns unhealthy or the container crash-loops, schema still behind because the image is older than the checkout, version unreadable) print the manual `docker compose restart backend` step and exit 1; they are reviewed, not exercised by a test.' No IT or unit test asserts a non-zero exit or the manual-step text.
findings.suggestion: Add at least one IT for a post-commit failure. Example: start a backend image built without V4 (or `docker compose stop` after the restart starts) and assert exit 1 plus 'restart backend' and 'data is restored' in the output. Alternatively, extract the decision and health parsing into tools/lib and unit-test them from OperatorToolGuardTest.

findings.title: The tests for scenario 'Restored schema and checkout disagree without a restart' do not check that nothing was restarted
findings.evidence: Scenario THEN: '...warns that the dump is newer, and restarts nothing'. The newer-dump test only starts `db` (no backend service exists) and asserts `output shouldContain "V999"` and `"newer"`, so 'restarts nothing' holds trivially. The design's reason for not restarting (a running backend would ignore future migrations) is never exercised against a running backend.
findings.suggestion: Run the newer-dump case with the backend up and assert the output lacks 'restarted' and the backend container's StartedAt is unchanged. Or narrow the scenario to 'no backend running'.

findings.title: The health-wait loop's JSON.parse can throw, which exits with a stack trace and skips the 'data is restored' message
findings.evidence: Design decision 3: every failure after commit 'prints that the data IS restored plus the manual ... step, and exits 1'. backendHealthy() calls `.flatMap((line) => JSON.parse(line))` on `docker compose ps --format json` stdout without a try/catch. Any non-JSON line (a compose warning on stdout, or a format change) throws an uncaught SyntaxError after the restore has committed, so the operator sees a stack trace instead of the manual step. OperatorToolGuardTest already enforces 'usage, not a stack trace' for other inputs.
findings.suggestion: Wrap the parse in try/catch and treat a failed parse like `r.status !== 0` (retry, then fall through to fail(...) with the manual step).

findings.title: The printed manual restart command leaves out the compose file that the tool itself uses
findings.evidence: The tool runs `docker compose -f <ROOT>/compose.yaml [-p project] ...` (lib/compose.mjs composeArgs). The fallback it prints is `docker compose${opts.project ? ` -p ${opts.project}` : ""} restart backend`, with no -f. Run outside the backend checkout, that fails or targets a different compose project, which is exactly when the operator relies on it.
findings.suggestion: Build manualRestart from composeArgs(opts.project) (quote the path), or say 'run from the backend checkout'.

findings.title: Undocumented drift: the tool exits 1 on an unreadable version or an unknown backend state even when no restart may be needed
findings.evidence: The spec defines only three outcomes: older+running → restart or exit non-zero; older+stopped → note; newer → warn. The code adds two more exit-1 paths: `if (restored === undefined) fail(...)` (psql version read failed) and `running === undefined` → fail(...) (compose ps failed). Both are only in design.md decision 3, not in the requirement or any scenario.
findings.suggestion: Amend the 'Data volume and backup' requirement (or add a scenario) to cover these exit-1 outcomes, or keep them and note them in the delta so the store spec does not silently diverge.

findings.title: The MODIFIED requirement exists only in this repo's change delta; its presence in the docs-store spec could not be verified
findings.evidence: The delta rewrites the product requirement 'Data volume and backup' (store spec platform-foundation) with new SHALLs: Flyway version comparison, restart, and the storage note. contract/ has no matching text (a grep for 'Data volume and backup' under contract/ found nothing), and `openspec show platform-foundation --store doucko` could not be run here. AGENTS.md: product truth lives in the docs store.
findings.suggestion: Make sure the docs-store platform-foundation spec gets the same MODIFIED requirement (docs-store change, then bump contract/), or confirm that archiving the backend change is the agreed route for operator-tooling requirements.

result.reasoning:
I confirmed the mechanism in the code, but the trigger is less likely than the finding says.

**What the code does:** The parse is at `tools/restore.mjs:121`, not 118, inside `backendHealthy()`. `JSON.parse(line)` runs on every non-empty line of `docker compose ps --all --format json backend` stdout, and nothing catches it:
- There is no try/catch inside the loop.
- The caller at line 159, `if (restart.status !== 0 || !backendHealthy())`, has no try/catch either.
- There is no `process.on('uncaughtException')` handler.

A SyntaxError would therefore end the script with a Node stack trace. That skips `fail(...)` (lines 160-163), which is the path that prints "the data is restored … run `docker compose restart backend`". The script already committed the restore at line 75, so this does break the intent stated in the header comment (lines 18-19): a failed restart should print the manual step. The other failure paths are all guarded with status checks:
- `r.status !== 0` leads to `continue`.
- `query()` returns null on failure.
- `backendRunning()` returns undefined when compose cannot answer.

The parse is the only unguarded step in the post-commit path.

**Where the finding overstates it:**
- **Partial lines:** not possible. `spawnSync` returns stdout only after the process exits, so there are no partial reads.
- **Warnings:** Compose writes its warnings (for example "version is obsolete") to stderr, which this script passes straight through to the terminal (`stdio: [..., 'pipe', 'inherit']`). They never reach stdout.
- **Older array format:** handled by the `flatMap`.

**What can still trigger it:** a compose or plugin build that writes a non-JSON line to stdout with exit code 0, or a future format change. That is unlikely but possible, and the cost when it happens is the exact failure the design meant to prevent.

**Verdict:** the mechanism is real and unguarded; only the likelihood is overstated. The severity stays minor.

I refuted this one. The code matches the description, but none of the triggers it names can actually happen.

**What is true.** At `tools/restore.mjs:117-121`, `backendHealthy()` calls `JSON.parse(line)` on each line of stdout from `docker compose ps --all --format json backend`, with no try/catch. Nothing up the call chain catches it either: line 159, the top-level module code. So a non-JSON line would crash with an uncaught SyntaxError.

**Why the triggers don't occur:**
1. **Partial line: impossible.** `compose()` (line 40) uses `spawnSync` with stdout piped. `spawnSync` waits for the process to exit and returns the whole buffered stdout, so `r.stdout` can never hold a partly written line. Also, a non-zero exit is skipped by `continue` before any parsing (line 115).
2. **Plugin notices or warnings on stdout: not real.** Docker compose v2 writes warnings to stderr, and stderr is set to `inherit`, not piped. That covers "version is obsolete", missing env vars and pull/hint messages. Docker's "What's next" hints are not shown for `compose ps` and also go to stderr. With `--format json`, stdout carries only the JSON.
3. **A compose release with another format: already handled.** v2 before 2.21 prints one JSON array on a single line. v2.21 and later print one JSON object per line. The `.flatMap(JSON.parse)` handles both, as the comment on line 116 says. Empty output is filtered out by `.filter(Boolean)` and then returns false through `!c`. Compose v1 (`docker-compose`) is not reached through `docker compose`, and it has no `--format json` anyway.

**Impact even if it did fire.** By this point the script has already printed `restore complete: <file>` (line 80) and the restart-in-progress line (line 157). A crash would still exit non-zero. The operator would lose only the tailored manual-restart hint, not the knowledge that the data was restored.

**Conclusion.** Calling `JSON.parse` without a guard on external output is a fair robustness nit. But the finding gives no realistic way for a user to hit it, and the reasons it gives are wrong or already handled. I could not confirm a reproducible failure, so I'm marking it refuted.

The finding holds. In `tools/restore.mjs`, the destructive restore commits at lines 75–79, and `restore complete` is printed at line 80. Only after that, at line 136, does `const latest = latestMigration();` run. `latestMigration()` in `tools/lib/migrations.mjs:32-34` calls `readdirSync(dir)` on `MIGRATIONS_DIR` (`ROOT/src/main/resources/db/migration`), and nothing guards the call: no try/catch, no `throwIfNoEntry`, no existence check. Nothing in `restore.mjs` wraps it either. If the directory is missing or unreadable, Node throws ENOENT/EACCES as an uncaught exception. The process exits non-zero with a stack trace instead of going through `fail()`, so the operator never sees the manual-restart hint (`docker compose restart backend`), which the script gives for every other post-commit failure (lines 141, 153, 160, 167). Nothing earlier in the flow reads that directory, so it is not validated before the destructive step.

The path is hard to reach. The tool and the migrations live in the same repo, so the directory is missing only in odd setups such as a sparse checkout or a copied tools/ folder. That fits the reviewer's severity of minor and confidence of low. Still, the mechanism exists as described and does not fit the script's own error handling, so the finding is not refuted. The suggested fix is cheap and correct: compute `latestMigration()` before the pg_restore/psql step (it does not depend on the database), or wrap it and call `fail()`.

The code does what the finding says: `latestMigration()` (tools/lib/migrations.mjs:32-34) calls `readdirSync(MIGRATIONS_DIR)` with no guard, and restore.mjs:136 calls it after the commit and the "restore complete" output. But no real user can reach the trigger.

1. ROOT (tools/lib/compose.mjs:8) is the repo root, two levels above tools/lib. MIGRATIONS_DIR is `src/main/resources/db/migration` in that same repo. The same ROOT also locates `compose.yaml` (line 9), and every docker call before the commit depends on it.

2. A "moved tools/ copy" therefore has no compose.yaml next to it. The first docker step, `pg_restore --list` at line 52, fails and prints "nothing was changed" before anything destructive happens. So that case never reaches line 136.

3. The only remaining trigger is a checkout that has `compose.yaml` and a running stack but no migration directory. That is a hand-crafted sparse checkout of a single-developer repo where the directory is tracked. The backend can't even be built from such a checkout.

4. Even if it were hit, the impact is small. The data has already been restored and "restore complete" has been printed. The exit code is non-zero (an uncaught throw). The only loss is the friendlier restart hint.

The mechanism is real, but under an exploitability/reproducibility lens the path is effectively unreachable for a real operator. This is a hardening nit, not a correctness defect.

The finding holds up against the code. In tools/restore.mjs, `schemaVersion()` (lines 95-101) explicitly returns `undefined` when either psql query fails, because `query()` returns null on a non-zero exit (line 91). After the restart, line 165 calls `schemaVersion()` again. Line 166's `!migrated` is true for `undefined`, so it calls fail() with `label(undefined)`, which is "an unreadable version" (line 138), and the text then says "its image is older than this checkout. Rebuild and start it with npm run stack:up." So a failed read is reported as a stale image.

Nothing else catches this case. The earlier `undefined` check (lines 140-142) covers only the first read (`restored`), not the read after the restart. `backendHealthy()` only checks the backend container's healthcheck, not whether `docker compose exec db psql` works.

The path can happen: a transient compose/exec failure, or the db container restarting between the health check and the query. It is unlikely, though, because the db was used successfully moments earlier. Even so, the message is internally contradictory ("unreadable version … image is older") and sends the operator to rebuild the image when the real problem is a failed read.

The code is also inconsistent with itself: the first read handles `undefined` on its own path with the manual-restart hint, and the read after the restart doesn't.

Impact is limited. The data is already restored and the script exits 1 either way, so this is only a misleading diagnostic. Minor is the right severity.

The mechanism is real. In tools/restore.mjs, `schemaVersion()` (lines 95-101) returns `undefined` whenever `query()` gets a non-zero psql or `docker exec` exit. The pre-restart call at line 140 handles `undefined` separately and prints the "could not be read" message. The post-restart call at line 165 does not. Since `!undefined` is true, line 166 sends it into the same branch as a version that was read and is behind. With `label(undefined)`, the message at lines 167-169 reads "schema is at an unreadable version, not V<latest>: its image is older than this checkout. Rebuild and start it with npm run stack:up." That points the operator at an image rebuild when the real problem is a failed read. Nothing else guards against this: the `backendHealthy()` check before it only polls the backend container's state and never queries the db through psql.

Reachability is real but unlikely. It needs `docker exec ... psql` to fail just after the backend reported healthy, which usually means the db is reachable. It can still happen, for example through a transient exec or daemon error, a db container restart, or a connection limit being hit. Even then, the effect is only a misleading diagnostic plus exit 1. The data is already restored and the step that follows (stack:up) is harmless. So this is a real correctness bug in the error message, with low impact. 'Minor' fits.

I confirmed the finding against the code. In tools/restore.mjs, line 130 adds `-p ${opts.project}` to `manualRestart` when `--project` is set. The logs hint at line 162 is a hard-coded string, `docker compose logs backend`, with no `-p`. The actual restart at line 158 uses `composeArgs(opts.project)`, which passes `-f COMPOSE_FILE -p project` (tools/lib/compose.mjs:12-14). So with a non-default `--project`, a user who runs the printed logs command gets the logs of the default project's backend, not the stack that failed. The two hints in the same message are also inconsistent with each other. Nothing else in the file fixes this: `fail()` just prints the message. The path can be reached whenever `--project` is given and the restart or healthcheck fails. Severity stays minor because `--project` is mainly used by tests ("tests use their own" in compose.mjs), and the problem is a misleading diagnostic message, not wrong behaviour. The `-f` point is a smaller side issue and also applies to `manualRestart`, but the main claim about the missing `-p` holds.

Confirmed. tools/restore.mjs:130 builds manualRestart with `-p ${opts.project}` when --project is set. The failure message at lines 161-162 prints a hard-coded `docker compose logs backend` with no project flag. --project is a documented, user-facing option (usage at line 4/32, passed to parseArgs). compose.mjs notes that tests use their own project. So the path is reachable: run restore with --project X, the dump is behind the schema, the backend is running, and the restart fails or never becomes healthy. The printed logs command then resolves to the default project (named after the directory, here presumably the main `doucko` stack), not project X. The operator either sees another stack's logs or gets "no such service". Nothing guards against this elsewhere. The impact is limited to a misleading diagnostic hint: `logs` is read-only and the restart hint itself is correct. Neither hint includes `-f compose.yaml`, so both depend on cwd equally. That partial point in the finding is a shared limitation, not a difference between the two hints. Minor severity is appropriate.

Two things in the code contradict the claimed mechanism.

1. **The wait is not silent.** `compose()` (tools/restore.mjs:40) spawns docker with `stdio: ["ignore", "pipe", "inherit"]`, so stderr goes to the operator's terminal. A `docker compose ps` that exits non-zero always writes its reason there ("Cannot connect to the Docker daemon…", "no such service", "project not found"). Each failed retry at line 115 therefore prints the real cause every 2 s. The operator does not wait 5 minutes with no feedback, and the cause is not hidden.
